sections.name: 📦 Operations & Supply Chain (INFORMS: Management Science, M&SOM, Operations Research)

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Sales Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail
items.desc: Randomized field experiments with millions of users at a crossborder online retailer test GenAI in seven workflows; sales rise in most, by up to 16.3%, worth roughly $5 per consumer per year, driven by conversion rather than cart size, with no worse returns or ratings. [Management Science, published online 2026-11-06]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Today's paper asks a simple question: does generative AI actually make a retailer sell more? It's from Management Science, and note we're working from the abstract only.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Nice, because most evidence so far is lab studies. Here it's field experiments.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Right. Randomized experiments involving millions of users and products at a leading crossborder online retail platform, over 2023 and 2024. The platform put GenAI into seven business workflows: customer service, matching consumers to products, advertising, and seller services.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Sales go up in most workflows, with effects from no detectable impact to 16.3 percent. The size depends on how much the AI adds beyond what the firm already did. Across the four applications that worked, that's roughly five dollars of extra value per consumer per year.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Where does the gain come from?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Higher conversion rates, not bigger carts. The authors read that as AI reducing frictions in search, information, communication and personalization. And importantly, return rates and customer ratings didn't get worse.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: So no hidden cost of pushy sales. Any heterogeneity?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Yes, larger gains for less experienced consumers. Caveat: these are short-term effects at one platform, so generalizing needs care. Takeaway: well-placed GenAI can causally lift retail sales without hurting satisfaction.

items.title: Men see more career advancement in jobs with AI, as women lose ground
items.desc: New research examines how exposure to AI shapes the gender gap at work, reporting that men in AI-exposed jobs are advancing faster while women are losing ground. [Washington Post, published 2026-11-07]

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Hello, this is the AI Research Digest for November seventh, 2026. Today is dominated by the market rout around the AI trade, plus one solid field experiment on generative AI and sales.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: Let's start with the markets. Bloomberg describes a five point seven trillion dollar rout this week as AI bets unwound, and says the S and P 500 had its biggest weekly drop since April 2025.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: The trigger, according to several outlets, was the Democratic sweep in the midterms. The Washington Post says investors fear data center building will slow, and if the industry's investment math stops working, the broader economy could take a hit.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: The Wall Street Journal adds that systematic trades amplified the losses, calling it a wild week that brought AI investors to the brink. And the Financial Times reports that hedge funds and retail investors both fled the trade.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: There are knock-on effects too. The FT says copper, which had soared on forecasts of data center demand, fell on fears of an AI backlash.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: Yet money keeps flowing at the top. Bloomberg reports OpenAI closed about eleven billion dollars of a round valuing it at one point two five trillion, and the FT says Anthropic plans to press ahead with an IPO targeting one point five trillion dollars before Thanksgiving.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: On jobs, the New York Times says the evidence is mixed: white-collar industries most exposed to AI kept adding jobs in October, though growth was weak. Bloomberg suggests hiring may be shifting from the data center buildout toward consultants who implement AI.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: And a Washington Post piece on new research says men in AI-exposed jobs are advancing faster while women lose ground.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Another Post story offers a counterweight on energy: a new study finds data centers have had only a marginal effect on residential electricity prices so far.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: Now the research. A Management Science paper ran randomized field experiments with millions of users at a crossborder online retailer, putting generative AI into seven workflows.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Sales rose in most of them, by up to sixteen point three percent, worth about five dollars per consumer per year, mostly through higher conversion. Returns and ratings did not get worse, and less experienced shoppers gained most.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: That's a useful contrast to the market anxiety: concrete, measured gains at the firm level.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: One more: the FT asks why America seems to dislike AI, noting voter hostility to Big Tech shaped the midterms while attitudes in Asia are far more optimistic.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: That's the digest for today. Full summaries and the archive are on the web page. Thanks for listening.
